t: Parallel Courses II — Bitmask DP over Course Subsets
o: We must schedule $n$ courses into semesters of at most $k$ courses each, respecting prerequisite edges, minimizing the number of semesters. In Example 1 ($k=2$), courses 2 and 3 have no prerequisites so they go together in semester 1; course 1 needs both, so it takes semester 2 alone; course 4 then takes semester 3 — answer 3. In Example 2, course 1 has three prerequisites but we can only take two per semester, forcing 4 semesters. The key constraint is $n \le 15$: exponential-in-$n$ algorithms are fine, which strongly hints at representing the set of completed courses as a bitmask and doing dynamic programming over subsets.
k: With n <= 15, state = bitmask of already-taken courses; dp[mask] = minimum semesters to reach that set.
A course is 'available' when every prerequisite's bit is set in mask; any subset of available courses of size <= k can be taken next semester.
Enumerating only submasks that contain the lowest available course avoids counting the same partition multiple times and prunes the search.

a.n: Approach 1: Bitmask DP with full submask enumeration
a.i: For each reachable set `mask` of finished courses, compute the set of courses whose prerequisites are satisfied. Any subset of at most k available courses can form the next semester, giving transition dp[mask | sub] = min(dp[mask] + 1). Enumerating all submasks of the available set costs O(3^n) total across all masks, which is fine for n <= 15. This brute-force-over-subsets version is simple and clearly correct.
s: Build prereq[i], a bitmask of prerequisites for course i (0-indexed).
Initialize dp[0] = 0 and all other entries to infinity.
For each mask with finite dp, collect `avail` = courses not in mask whose prereq bitmask is a subset of mask.
Enumerate every submask `sub` of avail with popcount <= k and relax dp[mask | sub].
a.t: O(3^n + 2^n * n) — each mask enumerates all submasks of its available set (sum over masks is 3^n), plus computing availability per mask.

a.n: Approach 2: Bitmask DP with canonical-subset pruning
a.i: The previous approach re-explores many equivalent choices: when picking a subset of available courses, the order within one semester doesn't matter, yet different submasks leading to the same next state are relaxed repeatedly. Forcing every chosen subset to contain the lowest-numbered available course removes symmetric duplicates without losing optimality — any optimal schedule can be reordered so the smallest available course is taken as early as possible. This prunes a large constant factor from the 3^n enumeration.
s: Same setup: prereq bitmasks and dp over masks.
Compute the available set for each mask as before.
Let low be the lowest set bit of avail; enumerate only submasks of avail that include low and have popcount <= k.
a.t: O(3^n) worst case asymptotically, but with a substantially smaller constant due to skipping duplicate/symmetric subsets; availability computation adds O(2^n * n).

w: In an interview, start with the observation that n <= 15 screams bitmask DP, then present Approach 1 and mention the canonical-lowest-bit pruning as an optimization (Approach 2). Common pitfalls: forgetting that a semester may take fewer than k courses (e.g., when few courses are available), off-by-one errors converting 1-indexed courses to bits, and assuming a greedy in-degree strategy works — it does not, because sometimes you should take fewer than k available courses to unblock a high-value chain later. Edge cases: no relations at all (answer is ceil(n/k)), k >= n (answer equals the graph's longest path length in semesters). Follow-ups: what if k varies per semester, or if you must report an actual schedule (track parent pointers in dp).
